# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The expansion of transcatheter therapies for structural heart disease has created a growing need for large-bore vascular access in patients whose femoral and iliac arteries are too small, calcified, or tortuous to accommodate contemporary delivery systems [1,2]. Transcaval access—deliberate crossing from the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the abdominal aorta—has emerged as a creative solution that exploits the retroperitoneal space and the favorable hemostatic environment of the venous system [3,4]. First described in preclinical models and then translated to humans by Lederman and colleagues, transcaval access has become an established alternative for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and other large-bore interventions [5,6].

## Rationale and Anatomic Basis

Approximately 10–20% of patients evaluated for TAVR have unsuitable transfemoral arterial anatomy, prompting consideration of alternative routes such as transapical, transaxillary, transcarotid, transcaval, and direct aortic access [1,7]. Each alternative carries distinct trade-offs in invasiveness and complication profiles [8]. The transcaval approach is attractive because venous access is fully percutaneous and avoids thoracotomy or surgical cutdown [9]. The abdominal aorta and IVC lie in close apposition below the renal arteries, and crossing through retroperitoneal tissue—rather than into the peritoneal cavity—allows the surrounding tissue pressure and the low-pressure venous system to tamponade bleeding after sheath removal [3,10]. Pre-procedural computed tomography is essential to identify a calcium-free aortic target and to avoid interposed bowel or vessels [11,12].

## Technique

The procedure involves advancing a stiff guidewire energized by electrocautery, or a dedicated radiofrequency wire, from a catheter in the IVC across into a snare positioned in the aorta [5,13]. Electrification of a 0.014-inch guidewire backloaded into a coronary microcatheter is the most widely adopted crossing method, providing controlled tissue penetration [13,14]. Once aortic access is established, the large-bore sheath is advanced for valve delivery [6]. At completion, the aortocaval tract is closed using a nitinol cardiac occluder device, typically a duct or ventricular septal occluder, which permits residual tract flow into the lower-pressure IVC until sealing is complete [4,15]. Persistent tract flow is common and usually benign, frequently resolving spontaneously on follow-up imaging [16,17].

## Clinical Evidence

The prospective Transcaval Access for Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement study demonstrated procedural feasibility in patients without other percutaneous options, with high rates of successful access and closure [6]. Subsequent single-center and multicenter registries reported encouraging mortality and morbidity outcomes, comparable in many respects to other alternative-access strategies [18,19]. Comparative analyses have suggested that transcaval access may offer advantages over surgical alternative routes with respect to length of stay and avoidance of general anesthesia in selected patients [20,21]. Beyond TAVR, transcaval access has been applied to thoracic endovascular aortic repair, mechanical circulatory support device delivery, and other large-bore procedures requiring routes unavailable through conventional arterial access [22,23].

## Complications and Management

The principal concern is retroperitoneal bleeding, which may arise from incomplete tract closure or aortic injury [24]. Most bleeding is self-limited and managed conservatively, but a minority require transfusion, covered-stent deployment, or, rarely, surgical repair [25,26]. Careful patient selection using cross-sectional imaging to identify a suitable aortic crossing zone reduces vascular complications [11,27]. Reported adverse events also include arteriovenous fistula formation, though clinically significant fistulae are uncommon and often amenable to percutaneous closure [28]. Operator experience and standardized closure protocols have progressively improved safety, and dedicated commercial crossing and closure systems are being refined [29]. Long-term imaging follow-up confirms durable tract sealing in the majority of patients, supporting the biological soundness of the retroperitoneal closure concept [30].

## Conclusion

Transcaval access represents a mature, fully percutaneous alternative for delivering large-bore therapies in patients lacking adequate transfemoral arterial access. Its safety and efficacy have been validated in prospective and registry settings, and ongoing refinement of crossing and closure technologies continues to broaden its applicability across the spectrum of structural heart and aortic interventions [6,19,29]. With appropriate imaging-based patient selection and operator expertise, transcaval access can be performed with acceptable complication rates, offering a valuable option within the contemporary alternative-access armamentarium [20,30].
